metadata.title: The Top 15 Stocks in the S&P 500 Are Now 47% of the Value. In 2000 Bubble, It Was 27%

content.text:
A record 46.7% of the S&P 500's market value now sits in the top 15 stocks, The Kobeissi Letter reported, leaving the other 485 companies with 53.3%.
That share sits 19.5 percentage points above the 27.2% the same group held during the 2000 Dot-Com Bubble.
How Top-Heavy Is the Index Now?
Nvidia (NVDA) leads at 7.5%, followed by Apple (AAPL) at 7.1%, Alphabet (GOOGL) at 5.9%, and Microsoft (MSFT) at 5.6%.
Together, they hold 26.1%, while the 11 stocks ranked behind them add up to about 20.6%.
Meanwhile, the 434 smallest members together roughly match the five largest in value, a record gap.
The S&P 500 weights companies by market value, so rising prices lift the largest firms' share automatically.
Economist Peter Schiff's bear market warning cited 479 US stocks at 52-week lows.
Separately, Goldman Sachs says artificial intelligence (AI) shares are holding the index up.
Do the Top 15 Stocks Signal a 2000-Style Bubble?
Historically, the S&P 500 lost nearly 50% after its March 2000 peak, which makes that year the natural comparison.
Goldman says market breadth, or how widely gains are shared, sits at its weakest since the dot-com bubble.
Investor Michael Burry's market warning points to 2000 and 2008, when early resilience gave way to deeper losses. He calls the current mood denial and expects it to last six to nine months.
In contrast, Tom Lee, co-founder of research firm Fundstrat Global Advisors, sees AI in 1997 rather than 1999. His model puts a bubble peak near 2033, still years away.
Therefore, S&P 500 index funds now put nearly half of their money into 15 companies. The benchmark many treat as a proxy for the US economy increasingly tracks a narrow set of mega-cap firms.
Read the Original story The Top 15 Stocks in the S&P 500 Are Now 47% of the Value. In 2000 Bubble, It Was 27% by Darryn Pollock at beincrypto.com
